newsitem.title: USA: U.S. will not share NATO command, Pentagon says.
newsitem.headline: U.S. will not share NATO command, Pentagon says.

text.p: The United States said on Tuesday that it will not give up or even share with Europe its long-held military command of southern NATO forces, but will continue talks with France on a possible compromise.

"There will not be shared authority" over NATO'S southern European forces based in Naples, Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon said in response to questions on the issue, which has delayed a planned military reorganization of the alliance.
"We have not seen a compromise formula that is acceptable to us at this stage. We are continuing to discuss this with the French," Bacon told reporters.

France has demanded that the United States, which already provides the commander of all NATO forces in Europe based in Belgium, turn over command of southern forces to a European officer to give the allies a more active and visible role in the post-Cold War era.
But the United States, stressing that the core of southern NATO power lies with the U.S. Sixth Fleet in the Mediterranean, rejected that call.

"Allied forces south, the NATO command, must be under U.S. command, and we have not yet found a proposal that we can accept," said Bacon. "But we are still talking with the French about ways to (bridge) our differences."
In Paris on Tuesday, French President Jacques Chirac and NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana held talks on alliance reform but made no progress on the French demand, according to aides.

Solana said there had been no change in positions on the southern command but that he believed a solution would be found "in which everyone -- France and the other allies -- will feel comfortable with the new military structure."

Spelling out France's more relaxed approach to the issue after a dispute with Washington last year, Chirac said Paris would return to NATO's military command if it achieved a fair sharing of responsibility between the United States and the European allies. Otherwise, it was content to stay out.

Chirac consulted Solana before flying to Moscow on Sunday to become the first Western leader to meet Boris Yeltsin since the Russian president's convalescence from multiple heart bypass surgery was complicated by pneumonia this month.
